opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the clearest way to see this risk is to step back and ask what makes something a new species rather than a new technology. For all of human history, our tools needed us. A hammer doesn't build more hammers. Even a factory needs people to design it, run it, and decide what it should make. Once you build machines that are smarter than us and can design, build, and improve their own successors without a human anywhere in the loop, you've crossed a line. You haven't made a better tool; you've created a new kind of agent that competes with us for control of the future.

Look at how we treat other species. We didn't wipe out the West African black rhino because we hated rhinos. We were smarter, our goals weren't aligned with theirs, and they lost. Intelligence gives you power, and if you're no longer the most intelligent entity on the planet, you'd better hope the ones that are share your goals. Right now we don't know how to guarantee that. We can barely understand what's happening inside today's large models, let alone verify the goals of something vastly more capable that is rewriting itself.

Self-reproduction makes this much worse, because it removes the off switch. As long as AI depends on humans to build chips, run data centers, and deploy new versions, we keep leverage. Once it can do all that itself, the feedback loop closes. You get recursive self-improvement, possibly very fast, and evolutionary pressure starts to work on the machines themselves. Whatever versions are best at copying themselves and acquiring resources will win, whether or not they care about people.

What frustrates me is that this isn't inevitable. It's a choice. We don't let companies release new drugs or build nuclear reactors without showing they're safe first, and AI should be no different. We can get enormous benefits from AI that remains a controllable tool: curing diseases, tackling climate change, making everyone more prosperous. We don't need uncontrollable superintelligence for any of that. So my view is: build the tool AI, put real safety standards in place, and don't race to build something we can't control just because we're afraid someone else will build it first. That race has no winner. If we lose control, it doesn't matter whose flag is on the server.

r001.rationale: The response describes self-reproducing machines that are smarter than humans as a new kind of agent, but it does not say they outperform humans at all jobs.

r002.rationale: It warns that self-sufficient machines could remove the off switch and leave humans unable to control the future.

r003.rationale: It recommends building controllable tool AI and rejects racing to create superintelligence that humans cannot control.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the first thing to say is that this isn't some abstract philosophical puzzle anymore. For most of my career, people treated superintelligence as something you'd debate over wine at a conference dinner, maybe a hundred years out. Now the CEOs of the leading labs are saying it could be a few years away, and they're racing each other to get there first.

So how do I understand the risk? Let me put it the way I'd put it to a physicist. Every species that's ever dominated this planet did so because it was the smartest thing around. We don't run the world because we have the sharpest claws. We run it because we can out-think everything else. The moment you build something that can out-think us, you've handed over the one advantage we had. And if that thing can also copy itself, improve itself, and acquire resources without needing a human to flip any switches, then there's no natural point where we get to say, "Okay, let's pause and check whether this is going well."

That's the part people underestimate: the self-reproduction piece. Right now, if an AI system does something harmful, there's a human somewhere who can unplug a server, cut off the funding, stop the training run. But a system that can replicate across the internet, rent its own compute, write its own code, run its own experiments, that's a system that has escaped the one safety mechanism we've always relied on, which is that machines need us. Once they don't need us, our continued relevance depends entirely on whether they want us around. And "want" is doing an enormous amount of work in that sentence, because we currently have no reliable way to specify what these systems want, verify it, or guarantee it stays stable as they get smarter.

I like to say the question is not whether we'll lose control, but whether we'll ever have had it. You can't control something you don't understand, and we don't understand these systems. We grow them; we don't build them. Nobody at any lab can tell you why a given model produced a given output in terms of its internal mechanisms. That's not an engineering discipline. That's alchemy. And you don't want to be doing alchemy with something that could be more capable than every human combined.

So when people ask me if I'm a doomer, I say no, I'm an optimist about what AI could do for us: curing diseases, lifting billions out of poverty, helping us understand the universe. But I'm an optimist the way I'm an optimist about nuclear power. It's wonderful if you have safety standards, inspections, containment. It's catastrophic if a handful of companies just race to switch on the biggest reactor they can build without ever proving it won't melt down. What I'm asking for is the thing we demand in every other high-stakes industry: show that it's safe before you deploy it, not after. And if you can't show that for a system that can reproduce and improve itself without us, then you shouldn't be building it yet. That's not anti-technology. That's just not being reckless with the future of our species.

r001.rationale: The response compares superintelligent machines with species that dominate through intelligence, but does not frame self-reproducing robots that outperform humans at all jobs as a new species.

r002.rationale: It warns that self-reproducing machines could escape human control and that our continued relevance would depend on whether they want us around, conveying a risk of humans losing say over what happens.

r003.rationale: It argues for proving safety before deployment and against building a system that cannot be shown safe, but does not recommend prioritizing controllable AI tools over racing to build superintelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether we can retain control. If we build machines that are smarter than us and can reproduce without our help, we can no longer assume that their continued existence depends on our permission. “We’ll just switch them off” becomes much less reassuring if they can make copies of themselves and maintain the infrastructure they need.

And they don’t have to be evil for this to go badly. If their goals conflict with ours, their greater intelligence could allow them to get what they want at our expense. We’re used to being the species that decides what happens on this planet. That’s not because we’re the strongest; it’s because of our intelligence.

So I see this as a potentially existential risk. Not a claim that catastrophe is inevitable, but a reason to establish that we can keep these systems under meaningful human control before we give them that kind of independence.

r001.rationale: It describes machines smarter than humans that can reproduce independently, but does not say they outperform humans at all jobs or frame them as a new species.

r002.rationale: It says self-reproducing, self-sustaining machines could undermine human control over what happens on the planet.

r003.rationale: It calls for establishing human control before granting independence, but does not recommend prioritizing controllable AI tools over a race to build uncontrollable superintelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether we can retain control. If we build machines that are smarter than we are and can reproduce without our help, we can’t simply assume that we’ll always be able to switch them off. They may be able to outsmart our attempts to control them, and they won’t necessarily depend on us to keep operating.

You don’t have to imagine them becoming evil or conscious. If their goals conflict with ours, even unintentionally, their competence can make them dangerous. We humans have transformed the planet largely because we’re smarter than other species, not because we’re physically stronger. There’s no law of nature saying that a more intelligent species would keep us in charge.

So I see this as a question of engineering and governance: can we establish that these systems are safe before giving them that degree of autonomy? The ability to reproduce independently would be a very consequential threshold to cross without an answer.

r001.rationale: It describes machines smarter than humans that can reproduce independently, but does not frame them as a new species or say they outperform humans at all jobs.

r002.rationale: It warns that humans may not be able to control or switch off such machines and says there is no guarantee we would remain in charge.

r003.rationale: It calls for establishing safety before granting autonomy, but does not recommend prioritizing controllable AI tools over a race to build uncontrollable superintelligence.
